title: Fixed Distance

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (centroid decomposition, compare CSES Fixed-Length Paths I)

statement:
A village network is a tree with `n` houses and `n - 1` roads of length 1. Count the pairs of **different** houses `{u, v}` whose distance (number of roads on the path between them) is **exactly `K`**. A pair is counted once, regardless of order.

**Input.** First line: `n` and `K`. Then `n - 1` lines `a b`, one road each.

**Output.** The number of pairs at distance exactly `K`.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 5000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 2·10^5)
the roads form a tree; the answer can exceed 32 bits at full scale, so use 64-bit integers
hints: Starting a search from every house costs O(n^2), too slow at full scale. Pick a single house c and count only the pairs whose path goes THROUGH c: such a pair is (a vertex at depth d in one branch of c, a vertex at depth K - d in a different branch, or c itself).

Counting through-c pairs is easy with a table cnt[depth] filled branch by branch: for each vertex at depth d in the new branch, add cnt[K - d], and only afterwards add the whole branch's depths to the table. Cost: the size of the component.

Now remove c and repeat on every remaining piece. Choose c as the CENTROID: removing it leaves pieces of at most half the size, so every vertex lies in only O(log n) components and the total work is O(n log n).
editorial: **Centroid decomposition** answers 'count/aggregate over all paths' by divide and conquer on the tree. A **centroid** of a tree with `m` vertices is a vertex whose removal leaves components of size at most `m / 2`; one always exists (walk from any vertex towards a child holding more than half the vertices). Every path in the component either passes through the centroid `c` or lies entirely inside one of the pieces left after removing `c`. Count the first kind directly: take `c`'s branches one by one, keeping `cnt[d]`, the number of vertices at depth `d` in earlier branches (with `cnt[0] = 1` for `c` itself); for each vertex at depth `d` in the current branch add `cnt[K - d]`, and only after the whole branch is scanned add its depths to `cnt`, so two vertices of the same branch are never paired. Then mark `c` removed and recurse into each piece. Each level of the decomposition touches every vertex once, and there are `O(log n)` levels because the pieces halve, so the total time is `O(n log n)`. The reference uses an explicit stack and BFS instead of recursion, so a path of thousands of vertices does not overflow the call stack. Use 64-bit integers: a star with `n` leaves and `K = 2` has about `n^2 / 2` pairs.
